newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: ASEAN non-intervention needs change-Thai minister.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN non-intervention needs change-Thai minister.

text.p: ASEAN needs to reconsider cherished policies such as non-intervention in members' affairs as it becomes more assertive in maintaining regional security, Thailand's foreign minister said on Wednesday.

"As ASEAN becomes more open, as growing interdependence means events in one country can send shock waves throughout the region, we need to rethink some of our most basic assumptions, ranging from the meaning of development and cooperation to the implications of non-intervention," Prachuab Chaiyasan told a congress of diplomats, academics and businessmen.

Recent issues have trained a spotlight on the group's non-intervention policy, such as speculative attacks on ASEAN currencies that have caused investors to shy away from the region, and the political situations in Cambodia and Burma.
He said each member of ASEAN (Association of South East Asian Nations) must be ready for the organisation "to be a more active, assertive and responsible player".
"We must seek to become an influential player in the maintenance of regional security," he added.
Prachuab is attending ASEAN's 30th anniversary meetings.
The Thai minister, along with foreign ministers of the Philippines and Indonesia, recently put the non-intervention creed to the test as they attempted to mediate in Cambodia's political crisis.
Cambodia's admission into ASEAN has been postponed indefinitely due to the overthrow of First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh by Second Prime Minister Hun Sen this month.
Laos and Burma, along with which Cambodia was to be inducted, became ASEAN members on Wednesday. ASEAN also includes Malaysia, Singapore, Brunei and Vietnam.

Initially, ASEAN's overtures to Cambodia were not welcomed. Last week, Hun Sen rebuffed the three-minister mission led by Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas, saying foreigners should stay out of its affairs.
"If we don't join (ASEAN), it won't be the death of us," Hun Sen was quoted as saying.
But that stance appears to have wavered, even as ASEAN's members themselves are rethinking old policies.
Ung Huot, Cambodia's foreign minister and nominee to replace Ranariddh, said on Wednesday that Cambodia not only wanted to join ASEAN, but welcomed its mediation efforts.

Other Cambodians have also asked for help. "I think that it would be a mistake not to do anything in Cambodia," Kao Kim Hourn, executive director of the Cambodian Institute for Cooperation and Peace, told the ASEAN congress on Wednesday.
He predicted that if the crisis was left unaddressed, in the next six months "fighting...will spread and it may affect neighbouring countries".
Malaysia, which now occupies the chairmanship of ASEAN, has traditionally taken a firm position of not interfering in other countries' affairs.
But Anwar Ibrahim, deputy prime minister of Malaysia, wrote in the July 21 issue of Newsweek magazine that ASEAN must move "from being a largely reactive organisation to one that is proactive".

"We need to 'intervene' before simmering problems erupt into full-blown crises, like the one now unfolding in Cambodia. Perhaps it is now appropriate for ASEAN to seriously consider the idea of 'constructive interventions'," Anwar wrote.
Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Ahmad Badawi on Tuesday also said the decision to admit Burma was an opportunity for such engagement.
ASEAN has faced criticism for admitting Burma, whose human rights record has been criticised by Western nations.

He said ASEAN believed it would be more beneficial to get Burma "into the club", so that it could more effectively monitor and influence Rangoon.
